titleStmt.author: Mubashir Arain
Michael J. Campbell
Cindy Cooper

bibl.title: What is a pilot or feasibility study? A review of current practice and editorial policy

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: TWO LABELS AND WHAT THEY BUY - `pilot` and `feasibility` measured across 54 published studies, 12 registered studies, three funding bodies and seven journal editors, six years before the same team's framework abandoned the distinction they recommend here
span.quote: Twelve studies which were interventional pilot/feasibility studies and which included testing of some component of the research process were identified through the UKCRN Portfolio database. There was no clear distinction in use of the terms 'pilot' and 'feasibility'. Five journal editors replied to our entreaty. In general they were loathe to publish studies described as 'pilot'.

span.label: when it is legitimate to label a study a `pilot` or a `feasibility` study, and what a reviewer should expect to find inside one
span.quote: It has become apparent to us when reviewing research proposals that small studies with all the trappings of a major study, such as randomization and hypothesis testing may be labeled a 'pilot' because they do not have the power to test clinically meaningful hypotheses. The authors of such studies perhaps hope that reviewers will regard a 'pilot' more favourably than a small clinical trial.

span.label: evidence from four independent sources - published papers, a registered-study database, funder policy and journal editors - that the two labels are used inconsistently, plus a recommendation to adopt the NETSCC definitions
span.quote: We conclude that pilot studies are still poorly reported, with inappropriate emphasis on hypothesis-testing. We believe authors should be aware of the different requirements of pilot studies and feasibility studies and report them appropriately. We found that in practice the definitions of feasibility and pilot studies are not distinct and vary between health research funding bodies and we suggest use of the NETSCC definition to clarify terminology.

span.label: critique
span.quote: Some authors suggest that analysis of pilot studies should mainly be descriptive,[ 3 , 6 ] as hypothesis testing requires a powered sample size which is usually not available in pilot studies. In addition, inferential statistics and testing hypothesis for effectiveness require a control arm which may not be present in all pilot studies. However most of the pilot interventional studies in this review contained a control group and the authors performed and reported hypothesis testing for one or more variables. Some tested the effectiveness of an intervention and others just performed statistical testing to discover any important associations in the study variables. Observed practice is not necessarily good practice and we concur with Thabane et al [ 2 ] that any testing of an intervention needs to be reported cautiously.

span.label: a label that authors reach for to protect an underpowered study and that editors read as a warning, attached to studies whose promised follow-up happens eight times in ninety
span.quote: Lancaster et al [ 3 ] found that 50% of pilot studies reported the intention of further work yet we identified only 8 (8.8%) which were followed up by a major study. Of these 2 (25%) were published in the same journal as the pilot.

span.label: a repeat of a 2004 review across the same seven journals, a UKCRN Portfolio database search, a canvass of seven journal editors and three funding bodies
span.term: a repeat of a 2004 review across the same seven journals, a UKCRN Portfolio database search, a canvass of seven journal editors and three funding bodies
span.quote: The editors of five (out of seven) medical journals responded to our request for information regarding publishing policy for pilot studies. Four of the journals did not have a specified policy about publishing pilot studies and mostly reported that pilot trials cannot be published if the standard is lower than a full clinical trial requirement. The Lancet has started creating space for preliminary phase I trials and set a different standard for preliminary studies. Most of the other journals do not encourage the publication of pilot studies because they consider them less rigorous than main studies.

span.label: **THE LABEL IS A SHIELD FOR AUTHORS AND A LIABILITY AT JOURNALS, IN ONE PAPER**: `small studies with all the trappings of a major study ... MAY BE LABELED A `PILOT` BECAUSE THEY DO NOT HAVE THE POWER to test clinically meaningful hypotheses. THE AUTHORS OF SUCH STUDIES PERHAPS HOPE THAT REVIEWERS WILL REGARD A `PILOT` MORE FAVOURABLY THAN A SMALL CLINICAL TRIAL` - against `In general they were LOATHE TO PUBLISH STUDIES DESCRIBED AS `PILOT``. **The same word is worth more to the author and less to the editor**
span.quote: It has become apparent to us when reviewing research proposals that small studies with all the trappings of a major study, such as randomization and hypothesis testing may be labeled a 'pilot' because they do not have the power to test clinically meaningful hypotheses. The authors of such studies perhaps hope that reviewers will regard a 'pilot' more favourably than a small clinical trial.

span.label: AND THE NAMING ACT IS GIVEN AN ETHICS RULING: `It is generally accepted that small, underpowered clinical trials ARE UNETHICAL. THUS IT IS NOT AN EXCUSE TO LABEL SUCH A STUDY AS A PILOT AND HOPE TO MAKE IT ETHICAL.` A sentence about what a word cannot do - the corpus has definitions that decide funding and diagnosis, and this is the first that decides whether a study should have been run at all
span.quote: It is generally accepted that small, underpowered clinical trials are unethical [ 4 ]. Thus it is not an excuse to label such a study as a pilot and hope to make it ethical.

span.label: **AND THE PROMISE IS KEPT EIGHT TIMES IN NINETY**: `Lancaster et al found that 50% of pilot studies REPORTED THE INTENTION of further work yet WE IDENTIFIED ONLY 8 (8.8%) WHICH WERE FOLLOWED UP BY A MAJOR STUDY` - and `one would have EXPECTED ABOUT 45 ... WHEREAS WE ONLY FOUND 8`. The defining property of a pilot study is that a bigger study follows, and it does not
span.quote: Lancaster et al [ 3 ] found that 50% of pilot studies reported the intention of further work yet we identified only 8 (8.8%) which were followed up by a major study. Of these 2 (25%) were published in the same journal as the pilot.

span.label: AND THE REASON GIVEN INVERTS THE PURPOSE: `if THE PILOT SHOWS SIGNIFICANT RESULTS then researchers MAY NOT FIND IT NECESSARY TO CONDUCT THE MAIN TRIAL. In addition if the results are unfavorable or the authors find an unfeasible procedure, THE MAIN STUDY IS LESS LIKELY TO BE CONSIDERED USEFUL.` **A positive result cancels the trial and a negative result cancels the trial** - which leaves no outcome under which the study does what its name says
span.quote: The main reason given was that if the pilot shows significant results then researchers may not find it necessary to conduct the main trial. In addition if the results are unfavorable or the authors find an unfeasible procedure, the main study is less likely to be considered useful.

span.label: AND THREE PRIOR AUTHORITIES TREAT THE SECOND WORD THREE WAYS: Arnold et al `MADE USEFUL DISTINCTIONS BETWEEN: PILOT WORK which is any background research ..., A PILOT STUDY which has specific hypotheses, objectives and methodology and A PILOT TRIAL which is a stand-alone pilot study and includes a randomization procedure. THEY EXCLUDED FEASIBILITY STUDIES FROM THEIR CONSIDERATION` - while `Thabane et al ... INCLUDED `FEASIBILITY` OR `VANGUARD` STUDIES BUT DID NOT DISTINGUISH THEM FROM PILOT STUDIES`. Excluded, conflated, or split three ways
span.quote: They made useful distinctions between: pilot work which is any background research to inform a future study, a pilot study which has specific hypotheses, objectives and methodology and a pilot trial which is a stand-alone pilot study and includes a randomization procedure. They excluded feasibility studies from their consideration.

span.label: **AND THE LABELS DO TRACK THE METHOD, IN THE PUBLISHED LITERATURE**: `We found that studies labeled `FEASIBILITY` WERE CONDUCTED WITH MORE FLEXIBLE METHODOLOGY COMPARED TO THOSE LABELED `PILOT` ... `pilot` studies were reported with MORE RIGOROUS METHODOLOGICAL COMPONENTS like sample size estimation, randomization and control group selection THAN studies labeled `feasibility`.` Four of six components differ significantly by keyword alone
span.quote: We found that studies labeled 'feasibility' were conducted with more flexible methodology compared to those labeled 'pilot'. For example the term 'feasibility' has been used for large scale studies such as a screening programme applied at a population level to determine the initial feasibility of the programme. On the other hand 'pilot' studies were reported with more rigorous methodological components like sample size estimation, randomization and control group selection than studies labeled 'feasibility'.

span.label: **AND THEY DO NOT, IN THE REGISTERED-STUDY DATABASE**: `both pilot and feasibility studies included trials run as complete studies, including randomization, but with sample sizes smaller than would be intended in the full study and THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN THE TWO TERMS WAS NOT CLEAR-CUT.` **Two data sources in one paper, opposite answers to whether the words mean anything** - the published literature separates them by keyword and the registry does not, and the paper reports both
span.quote: However, both pilot and feasibility studies included trials run as complete studies, including randomization, but with sample sizes smaller than would be intended in the full study and the distinction between the two terms was not clear-cut.

span.label: AND THE DEFINITION THIS PAPER RECOMMENDS IS THE ONE ITS OWN AUTHORS LATER ABANDON: `We found the NETSCC definition to be THE MOST HELPFUL SINCE IT DISTINGUISHES BETWEEN THESE TYPES OF STUDY and to most closely mirror what investigators are doing.` **Michael J. Campbell and Gillian A. Lancaster are authors here and on eldridge2016**, which opens `We initially adopted MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE DEFINITIONS ... based on ... THE DEFINITIONS USED BY THE NIHR` and reports the panel voting them down 14-1
span.quote: We found the NETSCC definition to be the most helpful since it distinguishes between these types of study. In addition it was observed that most of the pilot studies report their results as inconclusive, with the intention of conducting a further, larger study. In contrast, several of the feasibility studies did not admit such an intention.

span.label: AND THE RECOMMENDED DEFINITION DRAWS ITS LINE AT THE OUTCOME: `CRUCIALLY, FEASIBILITY STUDIES DO NOT EVALUATE THE OUTCOME OF INTEREST; THAT IS LEFT TO THE MAIN STUDY. If a feasibility study is a small randomised controlled trial, IT NEED NOT HAVE A PRIMARY OUTCOME and the usual sort of power calculation is not normally undertaken.` A class defined by what it must NOT measure
span.quote: Feasibility Studies are pieces of research done before a main study. They are used to estimate important parameters that are needed to design the main study. For instance: • standard deviation of the outcome measure, which is needed in some cases to estimate sample size, • willingness of participants to be randomised, • willingness of clinicians to recruit participants, • number of eligible patients, • characteristics of the proposed outcome measure and in some cases feasibility studies might involve designing a suitable outcome measure, • follow-up rates, response rates to questionnaires, adherence/compliance rates, ICCs in cluster trials, etc. Feasibility studies for randomised controlled trials may not themselves be randomised. Crucially, feasibility studies do not evaluate the outcome of interest; that is left to the main study.

span.label: AND THE OTHER HALF DEFINES BY RESEMBLANCE: `A PILOT STUDY IS A VERSION OF THE MAIN STUDY THAT IS RUN IN MINIATURE to test whether the components of the main study can all work together ... IT WILL THEREFORE RESEMBLE THE MAIN STUDY IN MANY RESPECTS.` One class bounded by an omission, its sibling by a likeness - and eldridge2016 later keeps the likeness as the only differentia
span.quote: A Pilot Study is a version of the main study that is run in miniature to test whether the components of the main study can all work together. It is focused on the processes of the main study, for example to ensure recruitment, randomisation, treatment, and follow-up assessments all run smoothly. It will therefore resemble the main study in many respects. In some cases this will be the first phase of the substantive study and data from the pilot phase may contribute to the final analysis; this can be referred to as an internal pilot. Alternatively at the end of the pilot study the data may be analysed and set aside, a so-called external pilot.

span.label: AND PRACTICE IGNORED THE 2004 RECOMMENDATION IT WAS GIVEN: `Some authors suggest that ANALYSIS OF PILOT STUDIES SHOULD MAINLY BE DESCRIPTIVE, as hypothesis testing requires a powered sample size which is usually not available ... However MOST OF THE PILOT INTERVENTIONAL STUDIES IN THIS REVIEW CONTAINED A CONTROL GROUP AND THE AUTHORS PERFORMED AND REPORTED HYPOTHESIS TESTING ... OBSERVED PRACTICE IS NOT NECESSARILY GOOD PRACTICE.` A repeat review measuring whether its own field took the advice, and finding it did not
span.quote: Some authors suggest that analysis of pilot studies should mainly be descriptive,[ 3 , 6 ] as hypothesis testing requires a powered sample size which is usually not available in pilot studies. In addition, inferential statistics and testing hypothesis for effectiveness require a control arm which may not be present in all pilot studies. However most of the pilot interventional studies in this review contained a control group and the authors performed and reported hypothesis testing for one or more variables. Some tested the effectiveness of an intervention and others just performed statistical testing to discover any important associations in the study variables. Observed practice is not necessarily good practice and we concur with Thabane et al [ 2 ] that any testing of an intervention needs to be reported cautiously.

span.label: AND A CONSENT CONSEQUENCE FALLS OUT OF THE DEFINITION: `PARTICIPANTS IN SUCH STUDIES SHOULD BE INFORMED THAT THEY ARE IN A PILOT STUDY AND THAT THERE MAY NOT BE A FURTHER LARGER STUDY.` If the defining promise is kept 8 times in 90, then what a participant is told about why they are enrolled depends on a definition nobody in the field shares
span.quote: We have shown that pilot studies have different objectives to RCTs and these should be clearly described. Participants in such studies should be informed that they are in a pilot study and that there may not be a further larger study.

span.label: THE EDITOR SURVEY IS FIVE REPLIES OUT OF SEVEN AND THE AUTHORS SAY SO TWICE: `The editors of FIVE (OUT OF SEVEN) medical journals responded`, and later `THE VIEWS OF THE JOURNAL EDITORS, ALBEIT FROM A SMALL SAMPLE, were not particularly encouraging`. Four of the five had no written policy at all, so the finding is about absence of policy as much as about opinion
span.quote: The editors of five (out of seven) medical journals responded to our request for information regarding publishing policy for pilot studies. Four of the journals did not have a specified policy about publishing pilot studies and mostly reported that pilot trials cannot be published if the standard is lower than a full clinical trial requirement. The Lancet has started creating space for preliminary phase I trials and set a different standard for preliminary studies. Most of the other journals do not encourage the publication of pilot studies because they consider them less rigorous than main studies.

span.label: AND THE REGISTRY ARM IS TWELVE STUDIES: of 34 identified, `ONLY 12 STUDIES WERE INTERVENTIONAL PILOT/FEASIBILITY STUDIES WHICH INCLUDED TESTING OF SOME COMPONENT OF THE RESEARCH PROCESS. Of these 5 were referred to as `feasibility`, 6 as `pilot` and 1 as both` - and the component counts that follow (17 across 6 pilots against 6 across 5 feasibility studies) rest on those twelve
span.quote: For example, the 6 pilot studies reported the intention to evaluate a total of 17 methodological components whereas in the 5 feasibility studies a total of only 6 methodological components were specifically identified as being under investigation

span.label: **AND THE PAPER'S OWN NUMBER CELLS ARE UNRELIABLE, WHICH IS NOT OUR DAMAGE**: Table 3 reports participant ranges of `[8, 187777]` and `[5, 12774614]` - twelve million participants in a feasibility study - and Table 2 gives `76 [8, 1299]` under a header saying (IQR) while the prose says `median 76, INTER-QUARTILE RANGE (42, 216)`. Checked against the publisher's own XML: each is a SINGLE `<td>` cell, so the fusion is in the source. **No quantity from Tables 2-4 is tagged on this record**; the percentages ARE arithmetically consistent with their counts and only the participant-range cells are broken
span.quote: We conclude that pilot studies are still poorly reported, with inappropriate emphasis on hypothesis-testing. We believe authors should be aware of the different requirements of pilot studies and feasibility studies and report them appropriately. We found that in practice the definitions of feasibility and pilot studies are not distinct and vary between health research funding bodies and we suggest use of the NETSCC definition to clarify terminology.

span.label: AND THE FIELD'S PUBLICATION FILTER WORKS AGAINST THE EVIDENCE THE PAPER WANTS: `PILOT STUDIES, BY THEIR NATURE, WILL NOT PRODUCE `SIGNIFICANT` (i.e P < 0.05) RESULTS. We believe that publishing the results of well conducted pilot or feasibility studies is important for research, IRRESPECTIVE OF OUTCOME. There is an increasing awareness that PUBLISHING ONLY `SIGNIFICANT` RESULTS CAN LEAD TO CONSIDERABLY ERROR.` A class of study defined so that it cannot meet the criterion its journals apply
span.quote: Pilot studies, by their nature, will not produce 'significant' (i.e P < 0.05) results. We believe that publishing the results of well conducted pilot or feasibility studies is important for research, irrespective of outcome.. There is an increasing awareness that publishing only 'significant' results can lead to considerably error [ 7 ].

span.label: repeating a prior review's search terms, journals and time window exactly, and reporting the two periods side by side
span.note: eliminates: attributing a change in practice to a change in the reviewer's method · outcome: held
span.quote: Lancaster et al [ 3 ] found that 50% of pilot studies reported the intention of further work yet we identified only 8 (8.8%) which were followed up by a major study. Of these 2 (25%) were published in the same journal as the pilot.

span.label: adding a registered-study database arm, because `as many pilot studies are never published` the journal literature is a filtered sample
span.note: eliminates: publication bias in the sample of studies whose labels are being compared · outcome: partial
span.quote: However, both pilot and feasibility studies included trials run as complete studies, including randomization, but with sample sizes smaller than would be intended in the full study and the distinction between the two terms was not clear-cut.

span.label: canvassing the journal editors and funding bodies directly rather than inferring policy from what was published
span.note: eliminates: reading an editorial policy off the papers that survived it · outcome: partial
span.quote: The editors of five (out of seven) medical journals responded to our request for information regarding publishing policy for pilot studies. Four of the journals did not have a specified policy about publishing pilot studies and mostly reported that pilot trials cannot be published if the standard is lower than a full clinical trial requirement. The Lancet has started creating space for preliminary phase I trials and set a different standard for preliminary studies. Most of the other journals do not encourage the publication of pilot studies because they consider them less rigorous than main studies.

span.quote: They made useful distinctions between: pilot work which is any background research to inform a future study, a pilot study which has specific hypotheses, objectives and methodology and a pilot trial which is a stand-alone pilot study and includes a randomization procedure. They excluded feasibility studies from their consideration.

They excluded feasibility studies from their consideration.

span.quote: We have shown that pilot studies have different objectives to RCTs and these should be clearly described. Participants in such studies should be informed that they are in a pilot study and that there may not be a further larger study.

span.label: RCTs
span.quote: We have shown that pilot studies have different objectives to RCTs and these should be clearly described. Participants in such studies should be informed that they are in a pilot study and that there may not be a further larger study.

span.label: feasibility studies
span.quote: Feasibility Studies are pieces of research done before a main study. They are used to estimate important parameters that are needed to design the main study. For instance: • standard deviation of the outcome measure, which is needed in some cases to estimate sample size, • willingness of participants to be randomised, • willingness of clinicians to recruit participants, • number of eligible patients, • characteristics of the proposed outcome measure and in some cases feasibility studies might involve designing a suitable outcome measure, • follow-up rates, response rates to questionnaires, adherence/compliance rates, ICCs in cluster trials, etc. Feasibility studies for randomised controlled trials may not themselves be randomised. Crucially, feasibility studies do not evaluate the outcome of interest; that is left to the main study.

span.quote: Feasibility Studies are pieces of research done before a main study. They are used to estimate important parameters that are needed to design the main study. For instance: • standard deviation of the outcome measure, which is needed in some cases to estimate sample size, • willingness of participants to be randomised, • willingness of clinicians to recruit participants, • number of eligible patients, • characteristics of the proposed outcome measure and in some cases feasibility studies might involve designing a suitable outcome measure, • follow-up rates, response rates to questionnaires, adherence/compliance rates, ICCs in cluster trials, etc. Feasibility studies for randomised controlled trials may not themselves be randomised. Crucially, feasibility studies do not evaluate the outcome of interest; that is left to the main study.

span.quote: It has become apparent to us when reviewing research proposals that small studies with all the trappings of a major study, such as randomization and hypothesis testing may be labeled a 'pilot' because they do not have the power to test clinically meaningful hypotheses. The authors of such studies perhaps hope that reviewers will regard a 'pilot' more favourably than a small clinical trial.

The authors of such studies perhaps hope that reviewers will regard a 'pilot' more favourably than a small clinical trial.

For example the term 'feasibility' has been used for large scale studies such as a screening programme applied at a population level to determine the initial feasibility of the programme. On the other hand 'pilot' studies were reported with more rigorous methodological components like sample size estimation, randomization and control group selection than studies labeled 'feasibility'.

span.label: `pilot` (the label, as authors use it) - reached for when a study `DOES NOT HAVE THE POWER to test clinically meaningful hypotheses`, in the hope that reviewers `WILL REGARD A `PILOT` MORE FAVOURABLY THAN A SMALL CLINICAL TRIAL`
span.quote: It has become apparent to us when reviewing research proposals that small studies with all the trappings of a major study, such as randomization and hypothesis testing may be labeled a 'pilot' because they do not have the power to test clinically meaningful hypotheses. The authors of such studies perhaps hope that reviewers will regard a 'pilot' more favourably than a small clinical trial.

span.label: `pilot study` (NETSCC, recommended here) - `A VERSION OF THE MAIN STUDY THAT IS RUN IN MINIATURE to test whether the components of the main study can all work together`; internal if its data join the final analysis, external if set aside
span.quote: A Pilot Study is a version of the main study that is run in miniature to test whether the components of the main study can all work together. It is focused on the processes of the main study, for example to ensure recruitment, randomisation, treatment, and follow-up assessments all run smoothly. It will therefore resemble the main study in many respects. In some cases this will be the first phase of the substantive study and data from the pilot phase may contribute to the final analysis; this can be referred to as an internal pilot. Alternatively at the end of the pilot study the data may be analysed and set aside, a so-called external pilot.

span.label: `feasibility study` (NETSCC) - research done before a main study to estimate design parameters, which `CRUCIALLY ... DO NOT EVALUATE THE OUTCOME OF INTEREST`
span.quote: Feasibility Studies are pieces of research done before a main study. They are used to estimate important parameters that are needed to design the main study. For instance: • standard deviation of the outcome measure, which is needed in some cases to estimate sample size, • willingness of participants to be randomised, • willingness of clinicians to recruit participants, • number of eligible patients, • characteristics of the proposed outcome measure and in some cases feasibility studies might involve designing a suitable outcome measure, • follow-up rates, response rates to questionnaires, adherence/compliance rates, ICCs in cluster trials, etc. Feasibility studies for randomised controlled trials may not themselves be randomised. Crucially, feasibility studies do not evaluate the outcome of interest; that is left to the main study.

span.label: `pilot work` / `pilot study` / `pilot trial` (Arnold et al) - a three-way split: any background research, a study with hypotheses and methodology, and a stand-alone pilot study with randomisation
span.quote: They made useful distinctions between: pilot work which is any background research to inform a future study, a pilot study which has specific hypotheses, objectives and methodology and a pilot trial which is a stand-alone pilot study and includes a randomization procedure. They excluded feasibility studies from their consideration.

span.label: replicates → Lancaster et al's 2004 review of pilot studies in the same seven journals for 2000-01, repeated here for 2007-08 to test whether its recommendations changed practice

On the other hand 'pilot' studies were reported with more rigorous methodological components like sample size estimation, randomization and control group selection than studies labeled 'feasibility'.

span.label: **THE LABEL IS A SHIELD FOR AUTHORS AND A LIABILITY AT JOURNALS**: `THE AUTHORS ... PERHAPS HOPE THAT REVIEWERS WILL REGARD A `PILOT` MORE FAVOURABLY THAN A SMALL CLINICAL TRIAL` against `they were LOATHE TO PUBLISH STUDIES DESCRIBED AS `PILOT``
span.term: **THE LABEL IS A SHIELD FOR AUTHORS AND A LIABILITY AT JOURNALS**: `THE AUTHORS ... PERHAPS HOPE THAT REVIEWERS WILL REGARD A `PILOT` MORE FAVOURABLY THAN A SMALL CLINICAL TRIAL` against `they were LOATHE TO PUBLISH STUDIES DESCRIBED AS `PILOT``
span.quote: It has become apparent to us when reviewing research proposals that small studies with all the trappings of a major study, such as randomization and hypothesis testing may be labeled a 'pilot' because they do not have the power to test clinically meaningful hypotheses. The authors of such studies perhaps hope that reviewers will regard a 'pilot' more favourably than a small clinical trial.

span.label: **AND THE DEFINING PROMISE IS KEPT 8 TIMES IN 90**: `one would have EXPECTED ABOUT 45 ... WHEREAS WE ONLY FOUND 8`
span.term: **AND THE DEFINING PROMISE IS KEPT 8 TIMES IN 90**: `one would have EXPECTED ABOUT 45 ... WHEREAS WE ONLY FOUND 8`
span.quote: Lancaster et al [ 3 ] found that 50% of pilot studies reported the intention of further work yet we identified only 8 (8.8%) which were followed up by a major study. Of these 2 (25%) were published in the same journal as the pilot.

span.label: AND BOTH OUTCOMES CANCEL THE MAIN TRIAL: `if THE PILOT SHOWS SIGNIFICANT RESULTS then researchers MAY NOT FIND IT NECESSARY TO CONDUCT THE MAIN TRIAL ... if the results are unfavorable ... THE MAIN STUDY IS LESS LIKELY TO BE CONSIDERED USEFUL`
span.term: AND BOTH OUTCOMES CANCEL THE MAIN TRIAL: `if THE PILOT SHOWS SIGNIFICANT RESULTS then researchers MAY NOT FIND IT NECESSARY TO CONDUCT THE MAIN TRIAL ... if the results are unfavorable ... THE MAIN STUDY IS LESS LIKELY TO BE CONSIDERED USEFUL`
span.quote: The main reason given was that if the pilot shows significant results then researchers may not find it necessary to conduct the main trial. In addition if the results are unfavorable or the authors find an unfeasible procedure, the main study is less likely to be considered useful.

span.label: **AND TWO DATA SOURCES IN ONE PAPER GIVE OPPOSITE ANSWERS**: the published literature separates the labels by method (`MORE FLEXIBLE METHODOLOGY COMPARED TO`), the registry does not (`THE DISTINCTION ... WAS NOT CLEAR-CUT`)
span.term: **AND TWO DATA SOURCES IN ONE PAPER GIVE OPPOSITE ANSWERS**: the published literature separates the labels by method (`MORE FLEXIBLE METHODOLOGY COMPARED TO`), the registry does not (`THE DISTINCTION ... WAS NOT CLEAR-CUT`)
span.quote: However, both pilot and feasibility studies included trials run as complete studies, including randomization, but with sample sizes smaller than would be intended in the full study and the distinction between the two terms was not clear-cut.

span.label: AND THE NAMING ACT GETS AN ETHICS RULING: `IT IS NOT AN EXCUSE TO LABEL SUCH A STUDY AS A PILOT AND HOPE TO MAKE IT ETHICAL`
span.term: AND THE NAMING ACT GETS AN ETHICS RULING: `IT IS NOT AN EXCUSE TO LABEL SUCH A STUDY AS A PILOT AND HOPE TO MAKE IT ETHICAL`
span.quote: It is generally accepted that small, underpowered clinical trials are unethical [ 4 ]. Thus it is not an excuse to label such a study as a pilot and hope to make it ethical.

span.label: AND THE DEFINITION RECOMMENDED HERE IS ABANDONED BY TWO OF ITS OWN AUTHORS SIX YEARS LATER: `We found the NETSCC definition to be THE MOST HELPFUL SINCE IT DISTINGUISHES BETWEEN THESE TYPES OF STUDY` - against eldridge2016's panel voting mutual exclusivity down 14-1
span.term: AND THE DEFINITION RECOMMENDED HERE IS ABANDONED BY TWO OF ITS OWN AUTHORS SIX YEARS LATER: `We found the NETSCC definition to be THE MOST HELPFUL SINCE IT DISTINGUISHES BETWEEN THESE TYPES OF STUDY` - against eldridge2016's panel voting mutual exclusivity down 14-1
span.quote: We found the NETSCC definition to be the most helpful since it distinguishes between these types of study. In addition it was observed that most of the pilot studies report their results as inconclusive, with the intention of conducting a further, larger study. In contrast, several of the feasibility studies did not admit such an intention.

span.label: AND A CONSENT CONSEQUENCE: `PARTICIPANTS ... SHOULD BE INFORMED THAT THEY ARE IN A PILOT STUDY AND THAT THERE MAY NOT BE A FURTHER LARGER STUDY`
span.term: AND A CONSENT CONSEQUENCE: `PARTICIPANTS ... SHOULD BE INFORMED THAT THEY ARE IN A PILOT STUDY AND THAT THERE MAY NOT BE A FURTHER LARGER STUDY`
span.quote: We have shown that pilot studies have different objectives to RCTs and these should be clearly described. Participants in such studies should be informed that they are in a pilot study and that there may not be a further larger study.

span.label: `A VERSION OF THE MAIN STUDY THAT IS RUN IN MINIATURE to test whether the components of the main study can all work together ... IT WILL THEREFORE RESEMBLE THE MAIN STUDY IN MANY RESPECTS`
span.term: pilot study (NETSCC, recommended by this paper)
span.quote: A Pilot Study is a version of the main study that is run in miniature to test whether the components of the main study can all work together. It is focused on the processes of the main study, for example to ensure recruitment, randomisation, treatment, and follow-up assessments all run smoothly. It will therefore resemble the main study in many respects. In some cases this will be the first phase of the substantive study and data from the pilot phase may contribute to the final analysis; this can be referred to as an internal pilot. Alternatively at the end of the pilot study the data may be analysed and set aside, a so-called external pilot.

span.label: `pieces of research done before a main study ... used to estimate important parameters ... CRUCIALLY, FEASIBILITY STUDIES DO NOT EVALUATE THE OUTCOME OF INTEREST`
span.quote: Feasibility Studies are pieces of research done before a main study. They are used to estimate important parameters that are needed to design the main study. For instance: • standard deviation of the outcome measure, which is needed in some cases to estimate sample size, • willingness of participants to be randomised, • willingness of clinicians to recruit participants, • number of eligible patients, • characteristics of the proposed outcome measure and in some cases feasibility studies might involve designing a suitable outcome measure, • follow-up rates, response rates to questionnaires, adherence/compliance rates, ICCs in cluster trials, etc. Feasibility studies for randomised controlled trials may not themselves be randomised. Crucially, feasibility studies do not evaluate the outcome of interest; that is left to the main study.

span.label: and 2 of those 8 appeared in the same journal as the pilot
span.term: pilot studies followed by a main study
span.quote: Lancaster et al [ 3 ] found that 50% of pilot studies reported the intention of further work yet we identified only 8 (8.8%) which were followed up by a major study. Of these 2 (25%) were published in the same journal as the pilot.

span.label: the pilot label attaches to studies testing more of the main trial at once
span.term: methodological components under investigation, registry arm
span.quote: For example, the 6 pilot studies reported the intention to evaluate a total of 17 methodological components whereas in the 5 feasibility studies a total of only 6 methodological components were specifically identified as being under investigation

span.label: `Most of the other journals DO NOT ENCOURAGE THE PUBLICATION of pilot studies BECAUSE THEY CONSIDER THEM LESS RIGOROUS than main studies`
span.term: journal editors responding, and their policies
span.quote: The editors of five (out of seven) medical journals responded to our request for information regarding publishing policy for pilot studies. Four of the journals did not have a specified policy about publishing pilot studies and mostly reported that pilot trials cannot be published if the standard is lower than a full clinical trial requirement. The Lancet has started creating space for preliminary phase I trials and set a different standard for preliminary studies. Most of the other journals do not encourage the publication of pilot studies because they consider them less rigorous than main studies.

span.label: `PILOT STUDIES, BY THEIR NATURE, WILL NOT PRODUCE `SIGNIFICANT` (i.e P < 0.05) RESULTS` - and most editors `do not encourage the publication of pilot studies`. The definition and the publication filter are in direct conflict, and the paper says so in the same paragraph as `PUBLISHING ONLY `SIGNIFICANT` RESULTS CAN LEAD TO CONSIDERABLY ERROR`
span.term: a class of study defined so that it cannot meet its journals' criterion
span.quote: Pilot studies, by their nature, will not produce 'significant' (i.e P < 0.05) results. We believe that publishing the results of well conducted pilot or feasibility studies is important for research, irrespective of outcome.. There is an increasing awareness that publishing only 'significant' results can lead to considerably error [ 7 ].

span.label: the only variable in the comparison - studies were split by which of two words appeared in the title or abstract, and then compared on sample size estimation, hypothesis testing, randomisation, blinding, control group and stated intent to continue
span.quote: We found that studies labeled 'feasibility' were conducted with more flexible methodology compared to those labeled 'pilot'. For example the term 'feasibility' has been used for large scale studies such as a screening programme applied at a population level to determine the initial feasibility of the programme. On the other hand 'pilot' studies were reported with more rigorous methodological components like sample size estimation, randomization and control group selection than studies labeled 'feasibility'.
